description: In London, Shakespeare wrote for the Globe. Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo: popular theater that became the high point of the English language.

hero.hook: An actor's playwright, a stage with no scenery, and lines that never die.

blocks.text: **William Shakespeare** (1564-1616) wrote for the London stage, not for the classroom. His plays mix kings, clowns, lovers, and murderers.
Four centuries later, he is still performed everywhere.

With the company of the [[Lord Chamberlain's Men]], he played at the [[Globe Theatre]], an open-air ring. The [[groundlings]] paid little and stood close to the stage. The theater was popular, loud, and alive.
Elizabethan London loved a show. Playhouses competed with sermons and bear-baiting. Shakespeare wrote inside that noisy market, not in an ivory tower.

blocks.caption: The Globe: a stage pushed into the crowd

blocks.text: He often wrote in Shakespearean blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter. Insults, poems, soliloquies. He invented words and built characters, Hamlet and Lady Macbeth among them, who became myths.
He recycled chronicles, Italian novellas, and older plays. His originality is in the language and the characters, not in inventing plots from nothing.
Several of his plays reached us only through the [[First Folio]] of 1623, published after his death.
He moved from laughter to blood. *Romeo and Juliet*, *Othello*, *King Lear*: families, power, jealousy. The history plays replayed England for an audience that liked seeing itself as an epic.
Comedies and tragedies answer each other. The fool tells the truth. The king goes mad. That mixing of tones is why he can still be staged in a thousand ways.

blocks.caption: The First Folio: saving the texts from oblivion

blocks.text: Translated, adapted, and sampled by cinema and rap, Shakespeare is still a toolbox for talking about ambition and desire. His secret: he wrote for actors, in front of a crowd.
To really grasp Shakespeare's theater, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Context counts as much as style. Dates, places, patrons, audience: all of it explains why a form appears at one precise moment, and not before.
Finally, a legacy is measured over the long run. What we see today in museums, films, or popular music still carries the mark of these inventions.
Translated in France and elsewhere from the 18th century on, he became a global classic. Every era finds its own mirror in him: romantic, political, postcolonial, feminist.
At the Globe, Shakespeare invented a popular theater whose characters and language went on to conquer the world.
